Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
People are not what they seem

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: For police violence, water/flooding and soil/outdoor smells are hard to reconcile as primary trauma-linked triggers when the rest of the profile contains no content suggesting a water, outdoor, or environmental trauma context. Bus riding could fit policing/public surveillance, but these other triggers point toward a different trauma setting.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells
issues.explanation: The appraisal of lost connection to community/culture is possible after police violence, but in this profile it is not supported by the selected triggers or memories, which center on acute sensory reliving and bodily threat rather than social exclusion, community rupture, or cultural shame. It feels disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, emotionless recall can coexist with reliving, but combining complete numb detachment with full multisensory reliving and bodily reenactment as parallel core memory experiences is somewhat tensioned. More importantly, the reliving items imply a very specific embodied trauma scene, yet the trigger set does not reflect cues plausibly tied to that scene.

issues.item: Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
issues.explanation: Mirror checking is difficult to explain from the rest of the profile. The threat items concern rapid bodily danger detection, reading faces, and sleep vigilance; the memories concern reliving; and the appraisals concern distrust/contamination/community loss. Mirror checking suggests appearance/body checking or checking for signs on oneself, but no associated appraisal or memory content supports it. It does not cohere well with the police violence formulation here.

vignette:
Priya is a 25-year-old South Asian counselor who works at a community mental health center. Six months ago, she was walking home from an evening shift when police officers stopped her, accusing her of matching a suspect description. They shoved her to the ground, pressed a knee into her back, and held her face against the soil. She was released without charges, but the smell of earth, the weight of the officer's body, and the sound of his voice stayed with her.

In the weeks after, Priya found that riding the bus-her only route to work-became unbearable. The moment she stepped on, the faint smell of outdoor dirt would trigger a full sensory reliving: she would feel the grit against her cheek, hear the shouted commands, and her body would stiffen into the same pinned position. And each time the memory surfaced, the danger felt immediate - as if the officers had just arrived and were about to give a command she would not be able to follow. This often happened before she had time to think; her body reacted to danger before her mind caught up. To cope, she started covering her face with her hands whenever she saw a police officer-even in a passing car-certain they could see the contamination she felt on her skin. That certainty made every step she took feel like moving through hostile territory - the threat was already inside her before she ever saw a uniform. She began checking mirrors constantly, scanning for anyone following her.

Priya came to believe that people are not what they seem, that even the most familiar face could hide threat. She studied passengers' body language, looking for signs of aggression. This hypervigilance, in turn, made the memory return more frequently: a sudden frown on a stranger's face would drag her back to the officer's expression as he leaned over her. Living in that constant state of alarm, she had come to accept that the world was as unsafe as she had first feared - and that she was too weak to withstand it. After the memory had broken through so vividly, she found she could no longer walk past a parked patrol car without her stomach dropping - the image had sharpened every edge of her world. She felt dirty, as if the event had permanently stained her, and this sense of contamination made her avoid friends she used to socialize with-she was certain they could see it, too, or that she no longer belonged in their world. Because she saw herself as marked, she started noticing police officers in places she had never registered them before - outside the grocery store, waiting at the crosswalk, parked in the lot behind the clinic. The isolation deepened her feeling of having lost her connection to community and culture, and that loss made every police encounter feel more threatening, more personal.

At night, she had difficulty falling asleep because she needed to stay alert; any creak or outside sound could trigger a flashback, and she would relive the moment with a strange numbness, as if it had happened to someone else, only to be followed seconds later by her body reenacting the position. That high alert meant that ordinary sensations - a car door closing, the whir of a bus engine, a shout from across the street - all became warnings she could not dismiss. But on nights when the alertness was at its peak, the memory surfaced on its own - not triggered by a sound, but pulled up by the body's readiness for danger. The memory itself drove her maladaptive strategies: after a full reliving on the bus, she would cover her face and avoid social eye contact, which then reinforced her belief that she was contaminated. The more she covered and avoided, the more isolated she became, and the more isolated she felt, the more she noticed police officers on every street corner.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was an incident on the bus last week. A passenger wearing a uniform triggered a severe reenactment-she froze, covered her face, and could not get off for two stops. Her supervisor at the counseling center saw her arrive shaken and urged her to talk to someone. Priya is afraid that she is losing her ability to do her job, where she once helped others process trauma. She hopes to stop feeling like a stranger in her own body and to reclaim the sense of belonging she has lost.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., feeling contaminated) directly cause an increased sense of threat.
No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to heightened perception of triggers (e.g., noticing police officers).
No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly drives a feeling of being in danger or threat.
No paragraph conveys that the memory itself makes the patient more sensitive to triggers (e.g., reminders).
No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat directly causes the intrusive memory to return.
No paragraph conveys that perceived threat leads to negative beliefs about oneself or the world.
No paragraph conveys that feeling threatened results in noticing or encountering more triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., feeling contaminated) directly cause an increased sense of threat.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals lead to heightened perception of triggers (e.g., noticing police officers).
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Threat: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly drives a feeling of being in danger or threat.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the memory itself makes the patient more sensitive to triggers (e.g., reminders).
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat directly causes the intrusive memory to return.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that perceived threat leads to negative beliefs about oneself or the world.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that feeling threatened results in noticing or encountering more triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
